reconciled_end: ## Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw — January 12, 2000
form: One signed opinion after argument. Part I states the common governing totality and review rules; Part II applies them to the supplied pre-stop record and affirms. The distinct application disagreement requires a dissent; the common rule is not enlarged into a categorical flight rule or a third-factor test. Form and propositions precede assignment counts.
compatibility: Stone and Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join the complete opinion and affirm. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas join the severable common rule in Part I but reject the application and would reverse/remand. Scalia accepts the controlling Ornelas allocation as the rule being applied without withdrawing his earlier disagreement; no new review-allocation holding is adopted. Neither camp relies on marked vehicles, an actual crowd, a witnessed transaction, race, proved recognition or the gun to supply a pre-stop fact. No frozen commitment changes.
kernel: Argued November 2, 1999; certiorari to the Supreme Court of Illinois, which sustained suppression after accepting the narcotics-area finding. The recovered original suppression testimony and clean validation supply the actual record. Nolan's uniform is established; the vehicle's markings, an actual crowd beside Wardlow, observation of all four cars, a transaction and pre-stop contraband are not. Looking toward the officers followed by running permits evaluation of a recognition inference but is not an admission. The firearm was discovered only after the initial stop and bag search. The granted question concerns the initial stop, not frisk validity. Flippo's actual later-search holding preserves separate authorization but does not decide this stop inference. The other effective earlier Records—Lesage, Fiore, Drye, Torres, Steamfitters and Kimel—change no stop or suppression premise. Paul, United Reporting and Hill have no effective event or count. Laidlaw, written earlier on January 12 for alphabetical assignment order, is counted but supplies no entering substantive authority for this uncoordinated same-day case. The January 12 group retains its common entering-law baseline, including the group continuing in the next chunk.
stone: The approved October 31, 2026 position requires affirmance under Terry's existing totality standard. Stone gives flight and the credited narcotics setting their relevant combined weight but finds the actual individualized inference insufficient. The original-record refinement does not displace that core: even allowing recognition to be inferred, the supported conduct and setting remain the insufficiency question; no new fact or categorical corroboration requirement is introduced. He joins the full majority and does not reach the separate frisk. No fallback is used.
continuity: The Illinois suppression judgment stands. The Court applies the existing totality standard and creates no additional reusable flight or third-factor test. The four dissenters' published application regards the immediate look-and-run sequence, route and credited narcotics setting as sufficient for an investigative stop, while preserving a separate frisk inquiry. Those application positions remain noncontrolling. O'Connor authors the published application dissent, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. Their sufficient-inference position does not change the all-nine common rule; Scalia's prior review-allocation objection remains noncontrolling.
sources: The clean original-record validation read the petition, both merits briefs and Joint Appendix in full. Its exact distinctions concerning testimony, trial inference and state appellate findings govern. JA 3–12 supplies the suppression testimony; the arrest-report time is only a state-court recitation. No missing source is treated as proof of litigant default. The final reconciliation confirms the eight Associates' preserved application split.

blocks.Event: Illinois v. Wardlow, No. 98-1036. Merits decision, January 12, 2000. Argued November 2, 1999. On writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of Illinois. The question is whether the actual pre-stop record supplied particularized reasonable suspicion after Wardlow looked toward officers and fled in an area associated with narcotics trafficking. The subsequent frisk and bag search are outside the granted question.
blocks.Participation: Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer participate.
blocks.Public Action: The Court affirms the Illinois Supreme Court's judgment sustaining suppression on the ground that the initial stop lacked reasonable suspicion.
blocks.Judgment & Remedy: Affirmed, 5–4. Supporting: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Opposing: O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas, who would reverse the initial-stop ruling and remand for any properly remaining issues. The existing suppression judgment remains in force; the Court does not separately decide the justification or scope of the frisk.

blocks.Holdings:
**I. Suspicion must remain individualized when flight and location are considered together.** Terry requires objective, particularized reasonable suspicion under the whole circumstances. Flight may contribute to that assessment, and a demonstrated connection between the location and crime may supply context, but location alone is insufficient and neither any flight nor every flight in a broadly described high-crime area creates a universal permission to stop.

**Authority:** Part I of {AUTHOR}'s opinion has all nine Justices' direct support as the governing law applied here.

**Controlling explanation:** Terry permits grounded inferences rather than proof of an offense, while Brown v. Texas rejects substituting a neighborhood label for an individualized basis. A refusal to cooperate or departure from police is not automatically criminally suspicious. Ornelas requires independent review of ultimate constitutional sufficiency with respect for historical findings and due weight to supported local inferences; it permits no supplementation of testimony. The later discovery of a firearm cannot justify the earlier stop. This common rule leaves the Justices' disagreement about its application intact.

**II. This record does not establish the required suspicion.** Wardlow's observed departure and route, considered with the credited narcotics setting and a permissible police-recognition inference, do not supply a sufficiently particularized basis for suspecting him of wrongdoing on this record. The initial stop was therefore unlawful, and the Illinois judgment sustaining suppression is affirmed.

**Authority:** Part II of {AUTHOR}'s opinion has direct support from Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court credits the state high court's finding about narcotics activity and does not exclude flight from consideration. Nolan saw Wardlow look toward the officers and run through a gangway and alley, but observed no law violation or transaction. His description of customers and lookouts concerned what normally occurred in such areas; it did not place a crowd or such activity beside Wardlow on this occasion. Nolan's uniform is established, while vehicle markings and Wardlow's observation of the whole caravan are not. Even allowing an inference that he recognized police, the flight's significance and the generalized setting remained too ambiguous to connect this person adequately to suspected criminal activity. The contrary reading gives those circumstances more particularizing force than this testimony supports. The Court finds neither an innocent motive nor actual guilt, requires no observed completed offense, and adds no categorical third factor.

**Questions not reached:** The separate safety basis and scope of the frisk and bag search are not adjudicated. A stronger flight-related record remains governed by Terry's existing totality inquiry.
blocks.Precedent Treatment: Terry v. Ohio is applied without a new categorical flight or corroboration rule. Brown v. Texas preserves the insufficiency of location alone. Ornelas v. United States supplies independent ultimate review and due weight for grounded factual inferences; it is not authority to invent additional observations. Flippo v. West Virginia's separate-authorization principle is consistent with keeping the stop and later search distinct but does not decide the stop's factual sufficiency.
blocks.Law After Decision: The existing totality standard remains unchanged. This pre-stop combination is insufficient on the supported record; flight remains relevant in other factually supported settings. The decision creates neither a right-to-flee exclusion of all evidentiary weight nor a mandatory third circumstance beyond flight and location.
blocks.Separate Writings: Justice O'Connor, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, agrees with the governing totality rule but finds reasonable suspicion here. Wardlow looked toward the officers and immediately ran through a gangway and alley in the credited narcotics setting. For the dissent, that temporal sequence and evasive route provide the individualized conduct missing from a location-only stop. Police recognition can reasonably be inferred without proving that he noticed every vehicle, and an innocent explanation need not defeat every grounded investigative inference. The dissent assumes neither marked cars nor an actual crowd, transaction, pre-stop firearm or guilty motive; the trial court's racial observation supplies no suspicion. It applies Ornelas's controlling independent review while giving weight to supported local inferences; Scalia retains his prior objection to that review allocation. The four would reverse the initial-stop ruling and remand for any properly remaining issue, without automatically reinstating the conviction or deciding the separate frisk and bag search.
blocks.Procedure After Action: The Illinois Supreme Court's suppression judgment stands. No further ruling on the bag search or frisk is directed by this disposition.
blocks.Source Notes: The petition, Joint Appendix and party briefs supply the suppression testimony and the state decisions. Testimony establishing Nolan's uniform is distinct from an inferred recognition of police, and the general expectation of customers or lookouts is distinct from an observed crowd. The state high court accepted the narcotics-area finding. The firearm was discovered after the stop and cannot supply its predicate.
